newsitem.title: USA: Consumers seen helping economy to revive - MFS.
newsitem.headline: Consumers seen helping economy to revive - MFS.

text.p: U.S. consumer spending should pick up enough during the holiday season to stimulate the economy in fourth quarter, an investment analyst said.

At an investment outlook conference of MFS, a Boston, Mass.-based mutual funds family, Leslie Namberg, senior vice president and chief fixed-income officer of MFS Investment Management, said, "We think it will turn out to be a pretty good Christmas."
Namberg said that consumer confidence has been moving up. Frequently, he said, the savings rate moves down when confidence is high.
But, Namberg said, recently both of these trends have been moving up. Some people attribute this to changing demographics, tying the trend to the tendency of older baby boomers to save more.

"I think its still too early to make that call," Namberg added. But pointing to rising disposable income and falling personal consumption expenditures, Namberg said, "We think it would be very unusual for consumers to be making money and not be spending it."
Namberg said that consumer spending in the fourth quarter would not pick up enough to cause the economy to overheat.

Namberg said that MFS believes that the economic slowdown in the third quarter was just a pause in an overall extended pattern of growth. The one potential fly in the ointment could be the housing sector, he said.

Referring to two sharp, consecutive montly declines in housing starts (September and October), Namberg said, "If housing starts don't turn up, that could call into question our outlook for an economic rebound."

Namberg said the current inflation picture is remarkbly well behaved. He said that while consumer installment debt is up, interest payments as a percentage of personal disposal income are down, thanks in part to lower interest rates.
Observing that the inventory-to-sales ratio is fairly low, Namberg said that suggests that when the consumer starts to come back, "We'll get some pickup in production and growth."
Namberg referred to scattered labor market shortages, concluding that overall the economy presents "a pretty rosy picture," with a risk being upward pressure on wages.
Namberg added that he believes that the dollar is topping out. "We think you've probably seen most of the upside move on the dollar," he said.
Worldwide trends favoring the fixed-income environment include a focus on getting national budget deficits down as a percentage of Growth National Product, he said.
